title: The Battelle nitinol allegation and the Naval Ordnance Laboratory record
notes: Carries the NOL record (NASA SP-5110, NOLTR 61-75, the patent filed 1 December 1961) beside the Battelle allegation (do not undo).

lead.text: Researchers allege that Battelle Memorial Institute studied a shape-memory metal recovered at Roswell in 1947, and that its 1948-49 nickel-titanium reports for Wright-Patterson are missing from both archives. The federal record, including a NASA review Battelle itself wrote, credits nitinol to the Naval Ordnance Laboratory around 1961 and gives Battelle only a later subcontracting role.

summary.text: The allegation: Anthony Bragalia and others say Battelle's Wright-Patterson-sponsored nickel-titanium reports of 1948-49 are missing, and a 2024 video investigation by UAP Gerb argues, following Jacques Vallee's paper trail, that the alloy Battelle studied came from the Roswell crash and is now called nitinol. No document connects Battelle's alloy work to Roswell directly.

The record set beside it: NASA's 1972 review, the Naval Ordnance Laboratory's 1961 technical report, the Navy's 1961 patent filing and a 1969 NASA contractor report, which together date and attribute the alloy.

Battelle's documented part in the Air Force UFO effort is real and separate: it held the Project Stork contract behind Blue Book Special Report No. 14, one of its scientists wrote the 1953 Pentacle memorandum, and in 2022 the Oak Ridge laboratory it co-operates analysed an alleged 1947 crash specimen for AARO.

record.text: NASA SP-5110, written for NASA by Battelle in 1972, opens by crediting Buehler and Wiley of the U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory with developing the shape-memory alloys about ten years earlier, and explains that Nitinol stands for Nickel Titanium Naval Ordnance Laboratory.

The earliest Naval Ordnance Laboratory nitinol report in SP-5110's references is NOLTR 61-75 of 3 August 1961, and US Patent 3,174,851 by Buehler and Wiley, assigned to the Secretary of the Navy, was filed on 1 December 1961 and granted on 23 March 1965.

NASA CR-1433 of September 1969 records that the nitinol was supplied by Buehler at the Naval Ordnance Laboratory and that Battelle, as subcontractor to Goodyear Aerospace, processed the basic rod; it calls the laboratory's work a recent discovery. NASA commissioned both reports.

Project Stork was Battelle's Air Force contract AF-19741, begun on 31 March 1952, to provide consultants, improve interrogation forms and analyse sighting reports for the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson. Seven status reports survive and the set is known to be incomplete; the contractor's name is struck out in most copies and typed in only one.

Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 of 5 May 1955 analysed 2,199 objects and classed 434, or 19.7 per cent, as unknown. The report names no contractor anywhere on its face; the Battelle attribution rests on the Stork status reports, and AARO's history records that Battelle released it under ATIC's cover to keep its anonymity.

The Pentacle memorandum of 9 January 1953, addressed to Miles E. Goll at Wright-Patterson under Project Stork and later attributed to Battelle's H. C. Cross, proposes controlled experiments in which aerial activity would be secretly scheduled in observed areas. No signed original has been produced.

AARO contracted Oak Ridge National Laboratory, run by UT-Battelle, in 2022 to test a magnesium alloy specimen alleged to come from a 1947 crash. The laboratory assessed it as terrestrial and unable to act as a terahertz waveguide, while noting that its undocumented chain of custody leaves its origin unclear.

Battelle, founded in 1929 and based in Columbus, Ohio, runs or co-runs large federal laboratories: it holds the Pacific Northwest contract, co-operates Oak Ridge through UT-Battelle, and partners Stony Brook University in running Brookhaven. Its executive Mark Peters became MITRE's chief executive on 3 September 2024.

claimed.text: Anthony Bragalia and other researchers allege, as reported in 2009, that Wright-Patterson-sponsored Battelle reports on nickel-titanium alloy from 1948-49 are missing from both the Air Force and Battelle archives.

UAP Gerb's February 2024 investigation alleges that Battelle studied a shape-memory alloy found at the Roswell crash site, as documented by Jacques Vallee, and that Battelle worked with the Air Force from the 1950s to index UFO reports and quell public interest. The video cites retrievable records, including the Stork progress reports and Special Report No. 14.
John Brandenburg said on a 2025 podcast that there was a 1949 contract between Los Alamos and Battelle concerning nitinol, declassified by Battelle in the 1960s.

Jacques Vallee holds that the Robertson Panel of January 1953 was not briefed on the Pentacle proposals and that another group had already set the limits of what it could discuss. Jesse Michels has said on podcasts that the memo could not be raised around the panel, without citing a document for that.

The board infers institutional continuity from Battelle's presence at the 1950s analysis of Air Force UFO data, at the 2022-24 specimen analysis, and in supplying MITRE's chief executive; the connections are documented and the significance is inference.

contested.text: The federal literature does not support a Battelle 1948-49 lineage for nitinol: the review Battelle wrote traces the alloy to the Naval Ordnance Laboratory around 1962 and cites no Battelle nickel-titanium work before 1968. The missing-reports allegation stands as an allegation, unsupported by the records opened.
The alleged Roswell connection rests on a coincidence of timing between the 1947 recovery, the claimed 1948-49 work and the absence of the reports; no document joins them.

The accounts disagree on the sponsor: the board's allegation names Wright-Patterson, while Brandenburg names Los Alamos, for the same alloy in the same period, and no contract record has been opened for either.

Jeremy Rys dated the laboratory's first nitinol discovery to 1954; the laboratory is right on the federal record but the date is not, since no opened document places any of its nitinol work before 1961.
The one specimen actually tested was found terrestrial, a magnesium alloy with no evidence of extraterrestrial origin, though neither AARO nor Oak Ridge could verify where it came from.
The Pentacle memorandum is known through a transcription and Vallee's copy; its dating and authorship are graded Tier 2 because no primary record of the memo is cited.

questions: Did Battelle produce any nickel-titanium reports for Wright-Patterson in 1948-49, and if so, where are they? No contract record has been opened.
Was there a 1949 Los Alamos contract with Battelle, as Brandenburg says, and what did it cover?
Where are the Project Stork status reports that the surviving set refers to but does not contain?
Does a signed original of the Pentacle memorandum exist in Air Force or Battelle files?
What was the chain of custody of the magnesium specimen before AARO acquired it?
Were Battelle's Stork records ever federal records, and could they still be requested?
